sections.h2: Where is Jefferson County, Georgia, and how is it laid out?
sections.html:
Jefferson County is a large, thinly settled county in east central Georgia, with Louisville as its seat and largest city. It was created on February 20, 1796, and covers 530 square miles, of which 526 are land, according to Wikipedia.

Five cities share the map: Avera, Louisville, Stapleton, Wadley and Wrens. McDuffie, Richmond, Burke, Emanuel, Johnson, Glascock, Washington and Warren counties surround it. A small northern strip, along a line running southeast from Stapleton and just south of State Route 80, drains into the Brier Creek part of the Savannah River basin, and the rest belongs to the Upper Ogeechee sub-basin.

A single school district, the Jefferson County School District, follows the county line, so every address falls under the same system. In 2020 the Census Bureau counted every resident as living in a rural area, with a median age of 43.4.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about Jefferson County homes?
sections.html:
Homes here are inexpensive and the population is shrinking. The Census Bureau puts the median owner-occupied value at $105,400 for 2020-2024, and the estimated population in July 2025 was 15,011, down 4.5% from the April 2020 base.

The county had 18,403 people in 1980 and 16,930 in 2010, so the slide is long-running. In 2020 the census found 7,148 housing units, 13.7% of them vacant, which leaves a good supply of empty houses competing with yours. With that supply, a house with a clean tax record is easier to move than one carrying delinquent years.

sections.h2: Which Jefferson County office handles which question?
sections.html:
Send billing and payment questions to the Tax Commissioner and value questions to the Tax Assessor. The Tax Commissioner is at 736 Peachtree Street, Louisville, GA 30434, phone (478) 625-7736, open Monday to Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

  • Tax Assessor (Board of Tax Assessors): (478) 625-8209; takes returns, homestead applications, and appeals
  • Tax Commissioner: bills real property, personal property, motor vehicle, mobile home and timber tax
  • Clerk of Superior Court: record center for warranty deeds and the free FANS notification system; the clerk's office number on the county tax site is (478) 625-7922

The commissioners and the Board of Education set the millage rate. The Tax Commissioner does not set value or rate.

sections.h2: When are Jefferson County property taxes due, and what is the penalty?
sections.html:
Real estate and business personal property taxes are generally due November 15. A 10% penalty applies to anything not paid within 90 days of that deadline.

There is one carve-out: homesteaded property with a bill under $500 does not receive the 90-day penalty. If the tax stays unpaid, the Tax Commissioner has both the right and the responsibility to levy on the property, though the office describes that as a last resort.

  • Mobile and modular homes: April 1 on one county page, May 1 on another, so ask the office which date applies before you rely on either
  • Mobile home permits: the current year's tax must be paid in full to get a location permit
  • Motor vehicles: due by the owner's birthday

The county's tax site also describes a one-time state homestead relief grant that appeared as a line item on bills of owners with an approved homestead exemption. It did not apply to rentals or non-homesteaded property.

sections.h2: How do returns and homestead filing work in Jefferson County?
sections.html:
Every owner must file at least an initial return for taxable property held on January 1, and the window runs January 1 to April 1. For real property that return renews each year automatically at the prior year's value unless you add property or make improvements.

Personal property is different: the PT-50P return is due every year with the Board of Assessors, and the office warns that if you no longer own listed items you must tell the Tax Assessor or you will be taxed on them. A new return filed in the window that declares a lower value starts your appeal if the assessors reject it.

  • Homestead applications go to the Tax Assessor's Office, and first-time homeowners bring a copy of the warranty deed
  • The county accepts applications all year, but one received after April 1 applies to the next tax year
  • A granted exemption renews until you move, change ownership or seek a different exemption
  • If the Board of Assessors denies an application, you must be notified and may appeal

Local exemptions replace the State's when they are larger. Ask the assessor's office for the combined amounts in force.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Jefferson County assessment?
sections.html:
File a written appeal with the Board of Tax Assessors, which has to mail you notice of any value change. The county's general information page gives 45 days from the date of mailing; its FAQ page gives 30 days, so treat the date on your notice as controlling and file early.

Valid grounds are taxability, value and uniformity compared with similar properties. A complaint about the amount of tax levied is not an appeal ground. The assessors review their value again, tell you their decision, and if you are still unhappy the file goes to the County Board of Equalization for a hearing. A Superior Court appeal can follow, and arbitration is available as an alternative to the Board of Equalization. Ask the Board of Tax Assessors how to start arbitration.

sections.h2: What farm, timber and historic programs does Jefferson County list?
sections.html:
Qualifying farm and timber owners can pay on a lower base. Agricultural property used for bona fide farming can be assessed at 30% of fair market value instead of 40%.

  • Conservation use: agricultural, timber, environmentally sensitive or residential transitional land valued at current use rather than market value
  • Covenant: the owner agrees with the Board of Tax Assessors to keep the property in qualifying use for at least 10 years; applications are due by April
  • Standing timber: taxed only when sold or harvested, at 100% of fair market value times the millage rate
  • Historic property: preferential assessment for the building and up to two surrounding acres

Sellers with acreage should ask the assessor before listing, to learn what the 10-year covenant requires of a new owner.

sections.h2: What should I handle before selling a Jefferson County house with tax due?
sections.html:
Get the payoff from the Tax Commissioner in writing and settle it at closing. A bill that has aged past 90 days has already picked up the 10% penalty, and the office can levy on the property.

The county's warranty deed copies come from the Clerk of Superior Court's record center, and the clerk offers FANS, a free opt-in system that sends an alert when a record is filed against a property. Sign up before you list so you hear about any filing under your parcel. If you have owned the house for several years and skipped some bills, ask the office for each year's balance separately.

faqs.q: What is the Jefferson County, GA tax due date?
faqs.a: November 15 for real estate and business personal property. A 10% penalty applies to amounts unpaid 90 days after that.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Jefferson County Tax Commissioner?
faqs.a: Call (478) 625-7736 or go to 736 Peachtree Street in Louisville. The office is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

faqs.q: Is there a penalty for a small homesteaded bill in Jefferson County?
faqs.a: No. Homesteaded property with a tax liability under $500 does not receive the 90-day penalty.

faqs.q: What is the Jefferson County homestead deadline?
faqs.a: April 1. The county accepts applications year round, but a later one starts the following tax year.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Jefferson County valuation?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Assessor at (478) 625-8209. The Tax Commissioner at (478) 625-7736 handles billing and payments, not value.
